definition: A giant molecule made of many repeating units joined together. Natural examples include proteins and starch; synthetic ones include poly(ethene) and PVC.
msAccepts: large molecule of many repeating units
built from many small monomer molecules
msAvoids: calling it just a big molecule with no monomer link

definition: A small molecule that joins with many others to make a polymer. Addition monomers carry C=C; condensation monomers carry two reactive end groups.
msAccepts: small molecule joined into a polymer
msAvoids: saying only one monomer is needed in condensation

definition: Polymerisation in which monomers carrying C=C simply add onto each other, opening the double bond, with nothing else formed and nothing lost.
msAccepts: C=C double bond opens to join
msAvoids: saying a small molecule is lost

definition: Polymerisation in which two different monomers join alternately, expelling a small molecule — usually water, sometimes hydrogen chloride — at every junction.
msAccepts: small molecule lost when monomers join
msAvoids: confusing with addition, where nothing is lost

definition: A condensation polymer built from a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, stitched by ester groups. Examples: Terylene and PET; biodegradable members are biopolyesters.
msAccepts: condensation polymer of diol plus dicarboxylic acid
contains ester linkages in the chain
msAvoids: omitting one of the two monomer families

definition: The structural fragment inside the brackets of a polymer formula that repeats along the chain; its bonds extend outside the brackets to the next units.
msAccepts: part of the polymer that repeats
drawn in square brackets with subscript n
continuation bonds extend outside the brackets
msAvoids: confusing with the monomer before the double bond is restored

definition: The substance used to start addition polymerisation. It is consumed in the reaction, so it must not be called a catalyst.
msAccepts: used up / consumed in the reaction
msAvoids: saying it speeds the reaction without being consumed

definition: The addition polymer of ethene, commonly called polythene. Actually an alkane-like saturated chain that will not decolourise bromine water; LDPE bags, HDPE bottles.
msAccepts: saturated, does not decolourise bromine water
low-density for films and bags, high-density for bottles

definition: Carrying only single bonds, with no double bond left to react. Addition polymers are saturated because the monomers' C=C bonds are spent in the joining.
msAvoids: applying it to the alkene monomer
saying saturated molecules are unreactive in every way

definition: The addition polymer of propene, formerly called polypropylene. Stronger than poly(ethene); used for ropes and crates; recycling mark PP.
msAvoids: omitting the CH3 side-group on the repeat unit

definition: The addition polymer of chloroethene, better known as PVC (polyvinylchloride). Strong and rigid for pipes and windows; plasticisers make it flexible; an electrical insulator.
msAccepts: rigid for pipes; plasticisers add flexibility; insulator
msAvoids: omitting the chlorine atom on the repeat unit
saying plasticisers are part of the polymer chain

definition: An additive that makes a rigid polymer such as PVC flexible, opening uses such as sheet floor coverings and clothing.
msAccepts: an additive mixed with the polymer
enables flexible uses like floor coverings
msAvoids: calling it part of the polymer chain
saying it changes the repeat unit

definition: The addition polymer of tetrafluoroethene (CF2=CF2), known as PTFE or Teflon. Very unreactive because of strong carbon-fluorine bonds; non-stick coatings and chemical-resistant linings.
msAccepts: unreactive due to strong C-F bonds
msAvoids: saying fluorine's element reactivity transfers to the polymer
omitting the strong C-F bond reason

definition: Unable to be broken down by bacteria in the environment. Addition polymers are non-biodegradable because their strong covalent bonds make them essentially inert.
msAccepts: strong covalent bonds make it inert
msAvoids: saying it rots slowly like paper

definition: Disposal by burial in large holes in the ground. Cheap and free of toxic gases from the plastics, but ugly, smelly, space-hungry and the waste stays unchanged for thousands of years.
msAccepts: cheap, no gases produced from plastics
waste remains for thousands of years; uses large areas

definition: Disposal by burning. Requires little space and the heat can generate electricity, but it produces greenhouse gases, releases toxic gases such as CO and HCl, and leaves ash for landfill.
msAccepts: produces CO2 and toxic gases; ash still landfilled

definition: An alcohol molecule with one -OH group at each end. Ethane-1,2-diol (CH2OHCH2OH) and propane-1,3-diol are the chapter's examples; one of the two polyester monomers.
msAccepts: one at each end of the molecule
msAvoids: confusing with a mono-ol such as propan-1-ol

definition: A carboxylic molecule with one -COOH group at each end. Ethanedioic acid (HOOCCOOH) and hexane-1,6-dioic acid are the chapter's examples; the other polyester monomer.
msAvoids: confusing with an ordinary monocarboxylic acid

definition: The -COO- group formed wherever a diol and a dicarboxylic acid join in condensation polymerisation, with water expelled; the same group that defines esters.
msAvoids: confusing with the unreacted acid group

definition: A biodegradable polyester: a condensation polymer whose ester links let it break down much more quickly than ordinary polymers. PLA is the flagship example.
PLA, the biodegradable polyester made from lactic acid obtained from corn starch. Used for biodegradable plastic bags and in surgery for internal stitches.
msAccepts: lactic acid obtained from corn starch
used for bags and surgical stitches
msAvoids: saying it is an addition polymer
